newsitem.title: USA: Clinton looks to debate as last test of campaign.
newsitem.headline: Clinton looks to debate as last test of campaign.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton faces possibly his last major obstacle of the road to re-election on Wednesday when he faces off against Republican Bob Dole in the final presidential debate of 1996.

Leading Dole by a large margin in all recent public opinion polls, Clinton has been preparing for an onslaught against his ethical standards from the increasingly desperate Republican nominee, who is under pressure from advisers and senior party colleagues to throw everything at the president.

Dole gave clear warning of his intentions in a speech to San Diego businessmen on Tuesday, his toughest attack yet on the president. He said he had never questioned Clinton's personal life and would not now because nobody was perfect. However, his public record was fair game.

The Republican nominee argued that Clinton ran his administration on half truths and evasion. "The goal is always to conceal ethical failure, not confront it," Dole said. "We hear, not apologies, but alibis. The buck stops nowhere."

The 90-minute encounter at San Diego University is in the form of a "Town Hall Meeting" with questions coming from the audience of some 150 undecided voters. That may make life difficult for Dole on two counts: first, Clinton is a master of that kind of forum while Dole may struggle to connect. Second, the questions may not be conducive to the kind of all-out assault Dole seems to have in mind.

Clinton knows he merely has to avoid mistakes to emerge from the debate in a commanding position for the final 20 days of the campaign leading to Election Day, Nov 5. He is likely to fall back on the economic achievements of his first four years and avoid brawling with Dole.

Asked about Dole's attacks on his ethics, Clinton on Tuesday said: "He's been doing a lot of that and I'll have a chance to answer that at the appropriate time ... My view is this country is better off than it was four years ago and we have worked hard to make it so. And we've worked hard by concentrating on ideas and issues, not insults."
Analysts said Dole had boxed himself in by threatening tough talk in the debate, a tactic which could easily backfire among voters who say they are tired of politicians slinging mud at one another.
"What's worse for Dole? To say he's going to get tough and not to do it or to say it and do it?" said Samuel Popkin, a political analyst at the University of California, San Diego.
"He better not go too far for his own sake. Even if the election is over, he has his dignity and his place in history at stake," he said.

A late-breaking flurry of charges about questionable financial contributions to the Democratic Party and the Clinton administration by Asian businessmen has provided the Dole camp with new ammunition to fire at the president.

"And now we see new charges that this administration has allowed a wealthy Indonesian family to buy presidential access, and play a role in foreign policy, in exchange for contributions to the Democratic National Committee," Dole said.

Nothing Dole has tried so far has had much affect in the past eight months of campaigning. Voters were unmoved when he quit the Senate, they were unimpressed by his 15 percent income tax cut proposal and they were mostly underwhelmed by his selection of Jack Kemp as his vice presidential running mate.

Many have not paid much attention to a campaign that has rarely seemed like a real contest. The television audience for the first debate 10 days ago was 40 percent lower than four years ago. Even though 70 million people may tune in for Wednesday's encounter, that would be well down on the 97 million who watched the final debate of 1992.

Frank Newport, editor in chief of the Gallup Poll, said Dole had little option but to play the character card. "It is now viewed as his last hope, so I think it is probable Bob Dole will turn up the steam," Newport said. "But there's no way around the fact that Clinton looks good for re-election."

Reuters pollster John Zogby said that after eight straight days in which he had widened his lead, Clinton might be looking at a landslide victory that could carry Democrats back to a majority in one or both houses of Congress.
